title: Cationized gelatin nanosphere-mediated release-controlled RNA interference targeting mTORC1 protects against intervertebral disc degeneration

sections.title: 研究问题
sections.text:
《Cationized gelatin nanosphere-mediated release-controlled RNA interference targeting mTORC1 protects against intervertebral disc degeneration》：研究问题的原文依据。

【Introduction · p0060】We hypothesized that Rptor siRNA (siRpt in rats and siRPT in humans) incorporated into cGNS (siRpt@cGNS, siRPT@cGNS) would sustain RPTOR suppression, inhibit mTORC1, enhance autophagy, and ultimately attenuate intervertebral disc degeneration. We further investigated whether cGNS could achieve sustained, biocompatible gene silencing in vitro and in vivo, thereby overcoming biological and technological limitations of conventional lipofection-mediated RNAi approaches (Fig. 1).

【Introduction · p0035】Low back pain is a leading global cause of disability that profoundly affects the quality of life while imposing a considerable socioeconomic burden [[1], [2], [3], [4]]. Among its diverse etiologies, intervertebral disc degeneration is recognized as the principal contributor, particularly in the aging population [[5], [6], [7]]. Current conservative and surgical interventions, including anti-inflammatory drugs, physiotherapy, and spinal fusion, are largely palliative and do not restore disc structure or halt disease progression [5]. Therefore, there is an urgent need to develop biological strategies to slow or potentially reverse degeneration by directly targeting the underlying molecular mechanisms.

sections.title: 研究方法
sections.text:
《Cationized gelatin nanosphere-mediated release-controlled RNA interference targeting mTORC1 protects against intervertebral disc degeneration》：方法与研究设计的原文依据。

【Design and synthesis of cGNS are optimized for sustained siRNA release · p0090】To develop a biodegradable nanocarrier for sustained intradiscal siRNA delivery, acid-processed porcine skin gelatin (PI9) was chemically modified by conjugation with spermine to introduce cationic amine groups (Fig. 3A). Quantification using the trinitrobenzene sulfonic acid (TNBS) assay demonstrated an amine substitution rate of 42.6 mol%, confirming substantial cationization of the gelatin backbone. Modified gelatin was recovered as a porous solid after lyophilization (Fig. 3B) and subsequently processed into nanospheres using a coacervation-based method.

【Design and synthesis of cGNS are optimized for sustained siRNA release · p0095】To regulate structural stability and degradation behavior, glutaraldehyde (GA) crosslinking densities were systematically optimized. GA was added at 5–100 μL per 1 mL of gelatin solution, generating nanospheres with distinct degrees of crosslinking (Fig. 3C). As degenerative intervertebral discs are characterized by elevated collagenase activity, enzyme-responsive degradation was evaluated. cGNS maintained structural integrity in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) but underwent collagenase concentration-dependent degradation. Among the tested formulations, GA at 20 μL/mL exhibited an intermediate degradation profile, with neither excessively rapid nor overly delayed degradation (Fig. 3D). Therefore, GA concentration of 20 μL/mL was selected for subsequent experiments to balance particle stability and enzyme-responsive degradability, consistent with previous reports [40,43,44].

sections.title: 主要结果
sections.text:
《Cationized gelatin nanosphere-mediated release-controlled RNA interference targeting mTORC1 protects against intervertebral disc degeneration》：结果的原文依据；数值与适用人群以引文为准。

【Design and synthesis of cGNS are optimized for sustained siRNA release · p0100】Rptor siRNA was complexed with cGNS via centrifugation-assisted mixing to generate siRpt@cGNS (Fig. 3E). Loading efficiency analysis demonstrated that siRNA incorporation reached saturation at approximately 30 pmol/μg cGNS. Incorporation at 20 pmol/μg cGNS achieved near-maximal loading while minimizing unbound siRNA; therefore, this ratio was selected as the standard siRNA/cGNS formulation for subsequent experiments (Fig. 3F). Thus, the formulation condition was determined based on the maximum loading capacity of cGNS rather than by arbitrary dose selection.

【In vitro siRpt@cGNS facilitates sustained cellular uptake, intracellular trafficking, endosomal escape, and autophagy activation · p0125】To ensure physiological relevance, NP cells were isolated from coccygeal (Co) intervertebral discs of 12-week-old male Sprague–Dawley rats. Western blotting (WB) confirmed that early passage cells retained disc NP notochordal characteristics, including brachyury and CD24 expression [8], and only first-passage and second-passage cells were used (Fig. S2). To minimize potential off-target effects, three independent Rptor siRNA sequences were screened (Table S3). In WB, sequence 2 achieved the most robust reduction in RPTOR expression and was selected for all subsequent experiments (Fig. S3).

sections.title: 图表阅读
sections.text:
《Cationized gelatin nanosphere-mediated release-controlled RNA interference targeting mTORC1 protects against intervertebral disc degeneration》：图表的原始标题与说明。

【Fig. 1 · fig1】Fig. 1 Schematic overview of the release-controlled RNA interference platform targeting RPTOR and its protective mechanism against intervertebral disc degeneration.Gelatin was first cationized with spermine and then processed by coacervation to generate cationized gelatin nanospheres (cGNS). Rptor siRNA was subsequently incorporated into the positively charged cGNS through electrostatic loading to form siRpt@cGNS. Following the cellular uptake and endosomal escape, cGNS gradually degraded in a protease-responsive manner, enabling controlled intracellular release of siRNA over time. Released siRNA was incorporated into the RNA-induced silencing complex (RISC), resulting in degradation of Rptor mRNA and suppression of RPTOR expression. This sustained silencing modulated the PI3K–AKT–mTORC1 signaling axis, promoted autophagy, and suppressed apoptosis, senescence, and extracellular matrix (ECM) catabolism in disc NP cells. In the rat tail disc static compression model, intradiscal injection of siRpt@cGNS attenuated structural disc degeneration compared with siCtrl@cGNS treatment, indicating the disc-protective potential of this release-controlled RNA interference platform.

【Fig. 2 · fig2】Fig. 2 The mTORC1-associated transcriptional program is consistently enriched across five human intervertebral disc degeneration datasets.A Enrichment of the MSigDB Hallmark gene set HALLMARK_MTORC1_SIGNALING in degenerated versus control discs in each dataset, expressed as the NES from GSEA. Points indicate the NES. All five datasets showed positive enrichment, and significance based on Benjamini–Hochberg-adjusted p values is indicated (***adjusted p < 0.001, **adjusted p < 0.01, *adjusted p < 0.05, ns, not significant). B log2 fold changes in representative mTORC1-associated genes across the five datasets, including effector and target genes (RPS6, RPS6KB1, EIF4EBP1, EIF4E, EIF4B, HIF1A, SLC7A5, ODC1, VEGFA, and SREBF1) and the upstream activator RHEB. RPTOR (boxed row), encoding the mTORC1 subunit RAPTOR, was included as a reference and showed no consistent change. Cell color indicates the log2 fold change in degenerated versus control discs (red, upregulated; blue, downregulated). The log2 fold change and corresponding nominal p value are shown in each cell (***nominal p < 0.001, **nominal p < 0.01, *nominal p < 0.05); n.d., not detected. Datasets included GSE23130 (Affymetrix microarray), GSE165722 (single-cell RNA-seq, pseudobulk), GSE244889 (bulk RNA-seq), GSE199866 (single-cell RNA-seq, pseudobulk), and GSE56081 (Arraystar array with probe sequences reannotated to RefSeq mRNA). Each dataset was analyzed independently.

【Fig. 3 · fig3】Fig. 3 Preparation and physicochemical characterization of Rptor siRNA (siRpt) incorporated into cationized gelatin nanospheres (cGNS) (siRpt@cGNS).A Chemical structures of PI9 gelatin, spermine, and cationized gelatin. Cationization introduced abundant amine (–NH2) groups for electrostatic interaction with siRNA. B Macroscopic appearance of lyophilized cationized gelatin. C cGNS were generated using increasing glutaraldehyde (GA) concentrations (5–100 μL/mL). D Enzymatic degradation profiles of cGNS with different crosslinking densities in collagenase-containing solution and PBS (n = 3 independent experiments, mean ± s.d.). E Schematic illustration of siRpt@cGNS preparation via centrifugation-mediated siRNA incorporation. F siRNA loading capacity of cGNS. Incorporation reached saturation above 25 pmol siRNA per μg cGNS (n = 3 independent experiments, mean ± s.d.). G Cryo-TEM images of cGNS and siRpt@cGNS. Scale bars, 1 μm and 100 nm. H Size and zeta-potential distributions of cGNS and siRpt@cGNS, with quantification of apparent size and zeta potential (n = 3 independent experiments, mean ± s.d.). IIn vitro release profiles of siRNA from siRpt@cGNS in PBS or collagenase-containing solution (n = 3 independent experiments, mean ± s.d.). J Gel-retardation assay of siRpt@cGNS prepared at increasing siRNA-to-cGNS loading ratios, including 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, and 30 pmol siRNA per μg cGNS, with quantification of freely migrating siRNA (n = 3 independent experiments, mean ± s.d.). K Heparin displacement assay of siRpt@cGNS at increasing heparin-to-siRNA weight ratios, with quantification of displaced free siRNA (n = 3 independent experiments, mean ± s.d.). Statistical significance in F, J, and K was determined using one-way ANOVA followed by Dunnett's multiple comparison test.
